sources.title: Climate Change and Peacebuilding in Fiji
sources.organization: Conciliation Resources, with Transcend Oceania and the Pacific Centre for Peacebuilding
geographic_coverage: Qauia, Nanuku and Maravu near Suva
sources.temporal_coverage: Fiji programme ran January 2020–June 2024; practice paper cover dated June 2024.
sources.limitations: Purposive implementer account, not representative or experimental.

sources.title: Perspectives on climate change and adaptation in Fijian villages contemplating relocation
sources.organization: Frontiers in Climate; Yuki Yoshida, Giles B. Sioen, Gauna Metuisela and Richard Crichton
geographic_coverage: Vanua Levu: Macuata and Cakaudrove provinces
sources.temporal_coverage: Qualitative village field visits in March 2024; published 4 September 2025.
sources.methodology: March 2024 qualitative field visits, interviews and talanoa across seven purposively selected iTaukei villages.
sources.limitations: Brief scoping sample centered on village leaders; not representative or causal; field notes summarize local accounts.

sources.title: Climate Change and Sea Level Rise, Fiji
geographic_coverage: Votua, Nawaqarua and Etatoko villages, lower Ba River Catchment, Viti Levu
sources.temporal_coverage: IMF paper completed 30 May 2025 and published June 2025; includes modeled sea-level-rise scenarios and earlier relocation cases.
sources.methodology: IMF staff estimates sea-level-rise costs and adaptation with CIAM; Box 1 summarizes prior village relocation research.
sources.limitations: Local cases are explicitly partial and anecdotal; CIAM requires finer topographic, population and asset data.

sources.title: Climate change and the planned relocation of people: A longitudinal analysis of Vunidogoloa, Fiji
sources.organization: Ambio; Celia McMichael, Teresia Powell, Annah E. Piggott-McKellar and Merewalesi Yee
sources.temporal_coverage: Seven qualitative research waves in Vunidogoloa from 2015 to 2023; journal issue June 2025.
sources.methodology: Longitudinal qualitative study with 41 interviews and 11 talanoa discussions over seven visits from 2015–2023.
sources.limitations: Single-village qualitative case; findings are residents’ accounts, not population estimates or causal effects.

claims.locator: PDF p. 10, climate change-induced (im)mobility and relocation priorities
claims.paraphrase: At publication, 42 communities sought relocation; Nabavatu and Cogea were top priorities; some TC Yasa-displaced families had lived in tents since 2020.

claims.locator: PDF p. 10, planned relocation consent thresholds and conflict risk
claims.paraphrase: Fiji’s SOP requires 90% consent to request relocation and 60% after scoping; CR warns the lower threshold may strain cohesion and escalate conflict.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The authors warn low consent can escalate relocation conflict.

claims.locator: PDF p. 11, Box 3 on informal settlements and climate change
claims.paraphrase: Seven-day discussions in Qauia, Nanuku and Maravu near Suva found climate impacts but not climate-driven migration; residents cited policing and mistrust as conflict drivers and tenure/service needs; report warns relocation could trigger conflict.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The paper warns relocation could trigger future settlement conflict.

claims.locator: PDF p. 6, governance, historical trust and political instability
claims.paraphrase: Fiji’s 1987, 2000 and 2006 coups affected community and civil-society trust and government engagement.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: CR ties coup-related trust to climate-governance engagement.

claims.locator: Results §3.1 and Table 2, community-specific climate impacts and relocation status
claims.paraphrase: Floods, cyclones and erosion damaged homes and land across the seven sites; flooding cut road access in Vunivau, Nacekoro and Dratabu, salt intrusion affected Vunidogoloa, and river erosion limited Matawalu farmland.
claims.limitations: Qualitative field accounts; no measured hazard prevalence.

claims.locator: Results §3.2 and Table 2, relocation and in-situ adaptation
claims.paraphrase: In March 2024, Matawalu, Nawaqarua and Nacekoro lacked relocation consensus; Vunivau and Nabavatu awaited government support, with procedural delay and tent shelters noted at Nabavatu.
claims.limitations: Relocation status is tied to the March 2024 field visit.

claims.paraphrase: Nawaqarua used early-warning alarms and drainage; Nacekoro planted mangroves and vetiver. Walls were sought at Matawalu, Nacekoro and Nawaqarua, but some walls elsewhere blocked drainage or prolonged floods.
claims.limitations: Strategies and unintended effects are qualitative community reports, not a comparative engineering assessment.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 9–10, Box 1, high-resolution coastal risk and Lomaloma map
claims.paraphrase: IMF staff’s map estimates that half of Lomaloma village on Vanua Balavu would be permanently flooded under a 1 m sea-level-rise scenario; mapped nearby retreat areas are hypothetical.
claims.scenario: 1 m above present sea level; IMF map shows possible retreat areas as hypotheses.
claims.limitations: This is a modeled scenario map, not a forecast of present inundation; the report says finer local data are needed.

claims.locator: PDF pp. 9–10, Box 1, household relocation experiences in lower Ba River Catchment
claims.paraphrase: IMF summarizes post-flood household surveys in Votua, Nawaqarua and Etatoko showing mixed relocation views; land ties, livelihoods, limited productive land and amenities, and tenure constrained resettlement; an Etatoko plantation lease was shortened for relocating households.
claims.limitations: IMF describes this review as partial and anecdotal; the household survey is cited from earlier research.

claims.locator: Full text, Results: knowledge of climatic risks and environmental security
claims.paraphrase: Residents of Vunidogoloa, Cakaudrove Province, recalled coastal and river flooding, erosion, rising tides and waves, salt intrusion and food insecurity; 26 households, about 140 people, relocated roughly 1 km inland in 2014 after seawalls failed.
claims.limitations: Residents’ qualitative recollections from one village; not an independent attribution study.

claims.locator: Full text, Discussion and Results on environmental risks, resources and services
claims.paraphrase: After moving, residents reported less coastal-flood exposure and better water, sanitation, schools and health access, but new cyclone and heat exposure, incomplete paths and drainage, and reduced fishing access, especially for women and older people.
claims.limitations: Reported changes are qualitative and uneven by gender, age and livelihood.

claims.locator: Full text, Local agency and participation; Discussion of relocation monitoring
claims.paraphrase: The relocation was community-initiated and led through village governance; later, residents reported no ongoing government or donor monitoring or formal channel for unfinished construction concerns, while the women’s committee continued village development work.
claims.limitations: These are reported local experiences, not an audit of agency or donor records.

search_audit.query: Fiji village coastal flooding relocation climate vulnerability Vunidogoloa Narikoso Nabavatu named communities primary study
search_audit.outcome: Frontiers reports named flood, erosion, cyclone, road-access and livelihood impacts across seven iTaukei villages; the longitudinal Vunidogoloa study adds repeated household accounts; IMF maps a conditional Lomaloma sea-level scenario and summarizes flood-related relocation barriers.

search_audit.query: Fiji climate relocation conflict land tenure community consent local governance conflict risks report
search_audit.outcome: Conciliation Resources explicitly identifies land/resource conflict, marginalization, relocation consent and governance as climate-related conflict mediators; it describes conditional cohesion risks and settlement-specific concerns without claiming widespread climate-driven violence.

search_audit.query: Fiji coups political instability community trust climate adaptation local governance relocation
search_audit.outcome: Conciliation Resources says historical political instability and coups shaped community and civil-society trust and engagement with government, relevant to climate-governance interaction. No inspected source establishes armed-insecurity effects on adaptation delivery or a nationwide FCV-to-climate pathway.

search_audit.query: Fiji community-led climate relocation resilience local adaptation early warning government community advocates
search_audit.outcome: Frontiers documents village alarms, drainage, mangroves, vetiver and locally managed responses; Conciliation Resources reports community advocacy and cross-ministry engagement. Baseline UNDP covers the 2026 early-warning initiative; UNDRR's full report PDF was not accessible beyond its publisher summary.

gaps: Conciliation Resources reports no large-scale unrest or violent conflict attributed to climate change in Fiji; it describes latent grievances, possible intra-community conflict and family violence, but the reviewed sources do not quantify their prevalence.
The Frontiers fieldwork is a purposive March 2024 scoping study; local statuses and adaptation accounts are not nationally representative and should not be treated as current.
IMF's Lomaloma result is a modeled 1 m sea-level scenario; local resettlement material is partial and anecdotal, not evidence for a nationwide retreat estimate.
The UNDRR early-warning publication was located, but its PDF body could not be accessed through the publisher's automatic-download endpoint; no new claim relies on its page summary.
No inspected source establishes conflict-related insecurity disrupting climate adaptation implementation or a national climate-conflict causal estimate.
